MOTION TO EXPUNGE LIS PENDENS
Tentative Ruling:
Motion to Expunge Lis Pendens:
“A lis pendens—also called a notice of pendency of action—is a document filed with a
county recorder that provides constructive notice of a pending lawsuit affecting the real property
described in the notice.” (Shoker v. Superior Court (2022) 81 Cal. App. 5th 271, 275.) The practical
effect is to cloud the property’s title and prevent its transfer until the litigation is resolved or the
lis pendens is expunged or released. (Malcolm v. Superior Court (1981) 29 Cal.3d 518, 523; Bishop
Creek Lodge v. Scira (1996) 46 Cal.App.4th 1721, 1733.) Recordation of a lis pendens is permitted
in any action in which the claimant has a “real property claim.” (CCP §405.1.) A “real property
claim” is a cause of action which would, if meritorious, “affect title to, or the right to possession
of, specific real property” or the “use of an easement.” (CCP §405.4.) A lis pendens is required in
an action to quiet title. (CCP § 761.010(b).)
A lis pendens may be ordered expunged on grounds, inter alia, that the complaint in the
action does not contain a “real property claim” or that the plaintiff cannot establish “probable
validity” of the claim by a “preponderance of the evidence.” (CCP §§405.3-405.32.) “Probable
validity” with respect to a real property claim, means that it is more likely than not that the claimant
will obtain a judgment against the defendant on the claim.” (CCP §405.3; see also Amalgamated
Bank v. Superior Court (2007) 149 Cal.App.4th 1003, 1012.) Expungement of an improper lis
pendens is mandatory. (CCP §§405.31-405.32; Amalgamated Bank, supra, 149 Cal.App.4th 1003,
1012.) While a motion to expunge under CCP §405.31 involves only a review of the adequacy of
the pleading and normally should not involve evidence from either side (BGJ Associates v.
Superior Court (2000) 75 Cal.App.4th 952, 957-58), a motion to expunge under CCP §405.32
requires the judicial examination of factual evidence. (Kirkeby v. Superior Court (2004) 33 Cal.4th
642, 649-50.) The burden of proof is on the party opposing the motion to expunge. (CCP §405.32.)
In opposing the motion to expunge the lis pendens, the claimant has the burden of proof and must
demonstrate the following: (1) the action, if meritorious, affects title to, or right to possession of,
real property (thereby constituting a real property claim); and (2) the probable validity of the real
property claim by a preponderance of the evidence. (Hunting World, Inc. v. Superior Court (1994)
22 Cal.App.4th 67, 70-71; see also CCP §§ 405.30-405.32.)
In this case, the parties do not appear to dispute that the action involves real property claims
that, if meritorious, would affect title to the Subject Property. The FAC includes causes of action
for quiet title, cancellation of instruments, declaratory relief and slander of title.

Purchaser argues that Plaintiff cannot establish the probable validity of her real property
claims because Purchaser is a bona fide purchaser for value without knowledge of Plaintiff’s claims.
In California, priority of title is based on a race-notice system, codified under Civil Code section
1214, which provides in relevant parts: “Every conveyance of real property... is void as against
any subsequent purchaser... of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a
valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded...” (Civ. Code, §1214.) “It is
well established that a bona fide purchaser for value who acquires his interest in real property
without notice of another’s asserted rights in the property takes the property free of such unknown
rights.” (Hochstein v. Romero (1990) 219 Cal. App. 3d 447, 451.) “The elements of bona fide
purchase are payment of value, in good faith, and without actual or constructive notice of another’s
rights. [Citation.]” “The absence of notice is an essential requirement in order that one
may be regarded as a bona fide purchaser.” (Gates Rubber Co. v. Ulman (1989) 214 Cal.App.3d
356, 364, emphasis in original.)
Purchaser purchased the Subject Property from a trustee’s sale on November 19, 2025, at
9:06 a.m., after placing the high bid of $150,000, (Decl. of C. Talkov, ¶ 3.) The Trustee’s Deed
Upon Sale transferring the Subject Property to Purchaser was recorded on December 5, 2025. (Id.
at ¶ 4; Ex. 1.) Purchaser asserts that she had neither actual nor constructive notice of Plaintiff’s
interest at the time of the purchase.
Plaintiff alleges that on May 29, 2025, the Trustee conducted a trustee’s sale whereby
Reyes placed the highest bid of $60,000. (FAC, ¶¶ 16, 17.) On June 13, 2020, Plaintiff submitted
a bid for $85,222.18 pursuant to Civil Code §2924m, which provides for an additional 15 days
after the trustee’s sale for certain eligible bidders, including eligible tenant buyers and prospective
owner-occupants, to submit bids before the highest bid at the sale becomes final. (Id at ¶ 18.) On
August 4, 2025, the Trustee recorded TDUS transferring the Subject Property to Plaintiff. (Id at
¶20; Ex. A.) On October 22, 2025, the Trustee recorded a Notice of and Rescission of Trustee’s
Deed Upon Sale pursuant to Civil Code § 1058.5(b).) (Decl. of S. Talkov, ¶12; Ex. 8.) As explained
below, this rescission restored the condition of record title to the Subject Property to the status quo
prior to the recordation of the August 4, 2025 TDUS.
On November 18, 2025, the day before the Trustee’s sale, Plaintiff attempted to record a
Notice of Pendency of Action under CCP § 405.29, which purported to give notice of the Reyes
Action, Case No. 2503909. (Decl. of S. Talkov, Ex. 4.) Plaintiff claims to be a cross-complainant
in the Reyes Action, although no cross-complaint was filed. (Id.) This lis pendens, which was the
only one recorded prior to the November 19, 2025 Trustee’s sale or December 5, 2025 recording
of Purchaser’s deed, does not give notice of Plaintiff’s claims. Nor does the second lis pendens
recorded by Plaintiff on December 11, 2025, which also notices only the Reyes Action. (Id. Ex.
3.) On December 29, 2025, Plaintiff recorded a Notice of Pendency of Action related to the present
case. (Id. Ex. 2.) However, when Purchaser purchased the Subject Property no lis pendens giving
notice of Plaintiff’s claims had been recorded. Plaintiff has not established that Purchaser had
actual or constructive notice of her interest in the Subject Property. Therefore, Purchaser is entitled
to bona fide purchaser status and takes the Subject Property free of any unrecorded interests.
Moreover, Plaintiff has not demonstrated the probable validity of her real property claims.
Plaintiff alleges the Notice of Rescission was invalid because Civil Code § 1058.5 does not apply
to deed based on bids obtained under Civil Code § 2924m. (FAC, ¶24.) Civil Code § 1058.5
provides:
Page 3 of 5
Where a trustee’s deed is invalidated by a pending bankruptcy or otherwise, recordation of
a notice of rescission of the trustee’s deed, which notice properly identifies the deed of
trust, the identification numbers used by the recorder or the books and pages at which the
trustee’s deed and deed of trust are recorded, the names of all trustors and beneficiaries,
the location of the property subject to the deed of trust, and the reason for rescission, shall
restore the condition of record title to the real property described in the trustee’s deed and
the existence and priority of all lienholders to the status quo prior to the recordation of the
trustee’s deed upon sale. Only the trustee or beneficiary who caused the trustee’s deed to
be recorded, or his or her successor in interest, may record a notice of rescission.
(Civ. Code § 1058.5(b), emphasis added.) Plaintiff does not provide any authority indicating that
this statute is inapplicable to Civil Code § 2924m.
Plaintiff argues that the Notice of Rescission was invalid because the Trustee’s authority
terminated once Plaintiff’s bid was accepted and the TDUS was recorded. Plaintiff cites no
authority for this, or any other argument raised in the Opposition. This assertion appears to
contradict the statute, which expressly grants the trustee who caused the trustee’s deed to be
recorded the power to record a notice of rescission. Thus, it expressly applies to deeds that have
already been recorded, presumably after a bid was accepted.
Plaintiff argues that this Notice of Rescission was invalid because the reason given for the
rescission is improper. Plaintiff contends that courts allow rescission only where the sale is void
due to: bankruptcy, court order, statutory nullity, fraud, failure of consideration or clerical
recording error. She asserts that Section 1058.5(b) does not independently authorize a trustee to
unwind a completed sale merely because the trustee later determines it made a mistake. Again,
Plaintiff cites no authority. The statute provides for rescission where the trustee’s deed is
invalidated by a pending bankruptcy or otherwise. (Civ. Code § 1058.5(b), emphasis added.) In
Bank of America v. La Jolla Group II (2005) 129 Cal. App. 4th 706, the court indicated that it was
not clear that the trustee’s deed had been invalidated when the trustors and beneficiaries had not
yet filed complaints, let alone obtained judgments challenging the sale; however, the court declined
to decide the question as moot. (Id at 717.)
The October 22, 2025, Notice of Rescission states that the reason for the rescission was
“irregularities occurred at the Trustee’s Sale auction resulting in confusion amongst bidders.”
(Decl. of S. Talkov, Ex. 8.) While the reason listed in the Notice of Rescission is vague as to the
irregularities and confusion, it appears that the rescission is based on the Trustee’s failure to
comply with Civil Code § 2924m. In her Complaint, Reyes alleges that the post-sale bidding
provisions under Civil Code § 2924m did not apply because she was a prospective owner-
occupant. (Reyes Comp., ¶7.) Reyes claims that she repeatedly informed the auctioneers of her
intent to occupy the Subject Property. Under section 2924m, if a prospective owner-occupant is
the last and highest bidder at the trustee’s sale, the sale becomes final on the date upon which the
conditions set forth in Section 2924h for the sale to become final are met. (Civ. Code §
2924m(c)(1).) Thus, it appears that, to extent the Trustee determined that Reyes as a prospective
owner-occupant, the TDUS in favor of Plaintiff was a statutory nullity under section 2924m.
Therefore, the rescission appears to be proper and restored the condition of title to status quo prior
to the recording of the TDUS. Plaintiff has not satisfied her burden of proving the probable validity
of her real property claims. The Motion to Expunge is granted.
Plaintiff's request for an evidentiary hearing is denied. Plaintiff was entitled to produce
evidence in support of her Opposition, as Purchaser did in support of the Motion. Plaintiff
apparently opted not to do so. As Purchaser notes, the issues are largely legal.
Attorney's Fees:
Pursuant to CCP $405.38, the court shall direct that the party prevailing on any motion
under this chapter be awarded the reasonable attorney's fees and costs of making or opposing the
motion unless the court finds that the other party acted with substantial justification or that other
circumstances make the imposition of attorney's fees and costs unjust. Purchaser requests
$12,247.50 in fees and costs based on 18.9 hours at $625/hour plus the $435 first appearance fee.
Plaintiff argues that she acted with substantial justification because the case involves novel
issues. It is true that there is little case law directly on point involving the application of Civil Code
§ 1058.5 to the circumstances of the present action. Plaintiff has established that her conduct was
substantially justified and no attorney fees are appropriate.
